meta.descriptionEn: October 1962. The world is a heartbeat from nuclear war. Deep under the Caribbean, a Soviet submarine called B-59 is cut off from Moscow, its air conditioning dead, its batteries nearly drained, while American destroyers drop depth charges overhead. The crew has no idea whether war has already begun. Aboard is a nuclear torpedo, and three officers who must agree before it can be fired. Two are ready. One is not. Who was Vasily Arkhipov, the quiet officer who had already survived the radiation disaster on K-19? What really happened inside that boiling steel hull? And is the famous story as simple as it sounds? Join us as we follow the evidence, the testimonies and the doubts behind one of history's closest calls.

Caribbean ke samundar mein Soviet submarine B-59 Moscow se kat chuki thi, garmi se bura haal tha, batteries khatam hone ko thin, aur oopar American jahaz depth charges gira rahe the. Submarine mein nuclear torpedo tha aur usay chalane ke liye teen afsaron ki razamandi chahiye thi. Do tayyar the, ek nahi. Vasily Arkhipov kaun tha? articleEn: On 27 October 1962, a Soviet submarine called B-59 lay hidden in deep water near Cuba. Above it, US Navy ships were dropping signalling depth charges to force it to the surface. Inside the boat it was hot and exhausting, and nobody knew whether war had already broken out in the world above.

Captain Valentin Savitsky came to believe that war might have started. He wanted to launch the submarine's nuclear torpedo, the T-5. But the captain's wish alone was not enough. Launching it required the agreement of three senior officers: the captain, the political officer and the executive officer. A debate followed, and only Vasily Arkhipov opposed the launch. He refused, and it is said that this refusal is why the nuclear weapon was never used.

Who was Arkhipov? What really happened inside the submarine that day? And how much can we trust the story? In this article we follow the whole story of that night, from Arkhipov's life to his decision and the questions raised about it. This is not just the story of one submarine. It is the story of a moment when a great deal of the world's fate rested on a decision among three men.

articleEn: Vasily Aleksandrovich Arkhipov was born on 30 January 1926 in Staraya Kupavna, near Moscow, into a Russian rural family. The boy from a village family would go on to become a vice admiral in the Soviet Navy. His journey began in the far eastern city of Vladivostok, where he studied at the Pacific Higher Naval School.

Then came August 1945, as the world was in the final days of the Second World War. He was aboard a minesweeper, a ship that clears explosive mines from the sea, and served in the Soviet–Japanese War. So even as a young man he had already taken part in real war. After the war he was sent to the Caspian Higher Naval School, also called the Azerbaijan Higher Naval School, and graduated in 1947.

His real career then began, and it was in submarines. He served on submarines in the Black Sea, Northern and Baltic Fleets, three separate fleets. By 1962 he had built up a great deal of experience of submarine life.

What was he like as a person? Most of what we know comes from his wife Olga. In the 2012 PBS documentary The Man Who Saved the World, she described Vasily as intelligent, well-mannered and very calm. He was known as a shy and modest man, and he rarely spoke about his most famous night. Olga said that even on holiday he would look for newspapers so he could stay as informed as possible about the modern world.

She also recalled a small incident. One day she saw Vasily burning a bundle of their love letters. He told her that keeping such letters would bring bad luck. In Olga's view, this suggests he was superstitious.

Picture it: a calm, shy officer who liked hunting for newspapers, and who would one day face an enormously heavy decision. But to reach 1962 we first need to see where the world stood at the time. How did the Cuba confrontation begin?

articleEn: Let us step back. The Cuban Missile Crisis lasted 13 days, from 16 to 28 October 1962, but its roots go back several years. In 1959 America installed Thor nuclear missiles in England, under Project Emily. In 1961 Jupiter missiles were placed in Italy and Turkey. According to sources, all of these were within range of Moscow. In April 1961 came the Bay of Pigs, when a force of CIA-trained Cuban exiles tried to invade Cuba and failed. Soviet leaders also worried that Cuba was slowly leaning toward China, with which Soviet relations were already souring.

In response to all this, a meeting between Nikita Khrushchev and Fidel Castro in July 1962 settled that nuclear missiles would be placed in Cuba. The aim was to deter a possible American attack. Another source says the two leaders had secretly agreed by May. The plan was code-named Operation Anadyr. Secrecy was vital, and the Russian word for it is maskirovka, meaning deception and concealment. Soldiers were even told they were going to a cold region, so they were issued winter gear such as ski boots and fleece-lined parkas. In the end a total of 43,000 foreign troops were brought to Cuba. On the night of 8 September the first shipment of R-12 missiles arrived, and work was under way at 9 sites.

America was growing suspicious. Since August, intelligence had been receiving reports of MiG-21 fighters and SA-2 anti-aircraft missile sites. Then, on 14 October 1962, a U-2 flight by Major Richard Heyser took 928 photographs, which showed an SS-4 missile site near San Cristóbal. The next day the CIA's National Photographic Interpretation Center analysed the images and found what looked like medium range ballistic missiles.

On 16 October President John F. Kennedy called together his key advisers, a group later named EXCOMM. Several options were debated: diplomacy, an air strike, an invasion, or a naval blockade. The Joint Chiefs of Staff were unanimous that a full-scale attack was the answer. But Kennedy feared that after an air attack on Cuba the Soviet Union might respond in Berlin, so he chose the less aggressive path.

On 22 October Kennedy ordered a blockade, but called it a quarantine so that America could avoid the formal legal status of war. That evening at 7:00 pm EDT he addressed the nation on television. He announced the presence of the missiles and described the quarantine. He said that any nuclear missile launched from Cuba against a country in the Western Hemisphere would be treated as a Soviet attack on America. During that speech, all US forces worldwide were placed at DEFCON 3, a sign of how serious the situation was.
All eyes were now on Khrushchev. But to understand our story we must look at another dangerous episode in Arkhipov's life: K-19.

articleEn: So let us go back a little in time. In July 1961 Arkhipov was posted to a brand-new submarine, K-19, a Hotel-class ballistic missile submarine. He became its deputy commander, the executive officer. The submarine was on exercises southeast of Greenland when a major leak suddenly developed in its reactor's coolant system. The cooling system stopped working, and there was no way left to cool the reactor. Radio communications failed at the same time, so the crew could not contact Moscow and had no way to call for help.

Imagine it: a nuclear submarine in the middle of the ocean, its reactor in crisis, and complete silence from the outside world. The crew had to decide for itself. Captain Nikolai Zateyev ordered seven engineers to find a solution. They had no backup system, so on the spot they built a secondary coolant system. The improvised fix worked and the reactor meltdown was stopped. All of this happened at sea, without outside help, and a single mistake could have meant disaster for the whole ship.

The price was very heavy. The entire crew, Arkhipov among them, was exposed to radiation. Those seven engineers and their divisional officer died within a month. We should remember their sacrifice with respect. Over the next two years another 15 crew members also died from the effects of radiation. The K-19 accident proved very costly. Arkhipov himself went through the same radiation, and when he developed kidney cancer many years later, some sources linked it to that exposure.

This is why the story of B-59 is incomplete without K-19. In one place a crew refused to give up; in the other, one man did. The accident gave Arkhipov a reputation, and according to sources that reputation carried weight in the B-59 debate of 1962. The story also reached the movies. In the 2002 film K-19: The Widowmaker, Liam Neeson played Captain Mikhail Polenin, a character influenced by Arkhipov's time on K-19. In other words, the film's hero was in reality a glimpse of a real officer.
In 1962 that same officer was aboard another submarine. This time the danger was not a reactor but a nuclear torpedo.

articleEn: Now back to October 1962. On the evening of 24 October the Soviet agency TASS published a telegram from Khrushchev. In it he warned that America's "outright piracy" would lead toward war. The Soviet Union regarded the blockade as aggression. The next day, 25 October, Kennedy replied that after repeated false assurances America had no choice but to act.

Meanwhile the blockade was being tested. An attempt was made to stop the tanker Bucharest, but it was judged to carry no military cargo and was allowed through. The Lebanese freighter Marucla was also stopped; its cargo was checked and it was allowed to continue. Kennedy claimed that 14 Soviet ships suspected of carrying offensive weapons had turned back.

At 10:00 pm EDT on 26 October the US raised Strategic Air Command readiness to DEFCON 2. B-52 bombers were kept on continuous airborne alert, the only confirmed time this has happened in American history. One eighth of SAC's 1,436 bombers were in the air. On the evening of 26 October Khrushchev's letter arrived, which Robert Kennedy described as very long and emotional. It offered to remove Soviet specialists in return for a guarantee not to attack Cuba.

But on the morning of 27 October a new message came over Radio Moscow. The condition had changed: the Cuban missiles would be traded for the Jupiter missiles in Italy and Turkey. Kennedy's advisers were confused, asking why the two messages differed so much. EXCOMM thought an internal debate was going on in the Kremlin.

Then came 27 October, which the White House later called Black Saturday. Around midday a U-2 was flying over Cuba, piloted by Major Rudolf Anderson. Over Banes a Soviet SA-2 missile shot his plane down and he was killed. The shot was fired on the orders of two Soviet generals, who had wanted permission from General Pliyev but could not reach him, perhaps because of illness. Kennedy had said earlier that he would respond to such an attack, but he decided to wait until a second one occurred. That same day Robert Kennedy told Soviet ambassador Dobrynin that the president was under military pressure and that events could move beyond his wishes.

Meanwhile another part of the story was unfolding in the deep sea. The Soviet Union had sent four Foxtrot-class submarines to the Caribbean, and one of them was B-59. It was diesel-powered, but it carried a nuclear-armed torpedo. The question now was what the tension on the surface would do down below.

articleEn: On 27 October 1962, in Caribbean waters, 11 US Navy destroyers and the aircraft carrier USS Randolph were tracking a Soviet submarine. This was B-59, a diesel-powered Foxtrot-class boat carrying a nuclear torpedo. She was in international waters near Cuba. The US Navy wanted to force her to the surface so she could be identified, and for this it dropped signalling depth charges. The Navy did not know at the time that B-59 carried a nuclear-tipped torpedo, which could be used if the submarine was damaged.

These were in fact practice depth charges, about the size of hand grenades. But Captain Savitsky took it as live ammunition being fired. For several days there had been no contact with Moscow. The crew had earlier heard American civilian broadcasts, but at depth it was not possible to pick up radio traffic, and when American ships are in pursuit a submarine stays deep. So B-59 was completely cut off from the world's news. The crew did not know whether war had begun above. That uncertainty was the most dangerous thing of all. Inside a submarine, time and news both stand still, and decisions are made on guesses.

Conditions inside were also getting worse. B-59's battery was almost exhausted and the air conditioning had failed. Picture a cramped submarine with no air conditioning, ringed by American ships. According to sources, conditions on board were extremely harsh. This was the day the White House called Black Saturday, when a U-2 had been shot down and the world stood at a delicate point. Soviet warheads were also present in Cuba without America's knowledge; sources give their number as both 162 and 158.

In these conditions Captain Valentin Savitsky felt that war might have started. His thinking was to use the nuclear T-5 torpedo. But could a captain decide this alone? No. Permission was required to fire a nuclear torpedo, and on B-59 the rule was even stricter. On most Soviet submarines with nuclear torpedoes, the approval of the captain and the political officer was enough, two people. But B-59 needed a third approval, because Vasili Arkhipov was aboard and he was also chief of staff of the brigade.

One clarification is needed: the actual commander of the brigade was Captain First Rank Vasili Naumovich Agafonov, not Arkhipov. Arkhipov was the brigade's chief of staff. So the decision rested in the hands of three men: Captain Savitsky, political officer Ivan Maslennikov, and executive officer Arkhipov. As a result, B-59 had an arrangement in which one man's refusal could stop a launch.

Why did the word of a second-ranking officer matter so much? According to sources, both his position and his reputation from K-19 carried weight. So what happens when only one of three refuses? That question leads us to the next part of the debate.

articleEn: Conditions inside the submarine were very hard and nerves were stretched. Captain Savitsky thought war might have begun and wanted to launch the nuclear T-5 torpedo. But on B-59 the captain could not decide alone, because the consent of a third officer was also needed. According to sources, a fierce argument broke out. Of the three officers, only one, Arkhipov, opposed the launch. Think about it: two officers on one side and one on the other. Had Arkhipov also said yes, history today might look very different.

This was not a calm conversation. The crew did not know whether war had begun, and there had been no contact with Moscow for days. Arkhipov was not only the executive officer. He was also chief of staff of the flotilla, so his word carried more weight. His standing from the K-19 accident had also been established, and that reputation helped him in this argument.

In the end Arkhipov persuaded Savitsky. It was decided to bring the submarine to the surface and wait for orders from Moscow. This decision is credited with preventing nuclear escalation. Conditions were also bad, since B-59's battery was almost exhausted. Not everyone agrees on every point, though. One later account describes the argument as less dramatic, and we will come back to that in the final section.

Along with the battery, the air conditioning had also failed. Conditions inside were harsh, and nobody knew what was happening outside. Then B-59 came up, and it did so among American warships. She carried a nuclear torpedo and was surrounded by 11 destroyers and an aircraft carrier. After surfacing she made contact with a US destroyer. So the moment passed in which the matter was settled by identification, not by gunfire.

Now another account. In 1997 Arkhipov recalled that after surfacing, American aircraft fired near his boat. By his memory, a plane passed over the conning tower and switched on powerful searchlights one to three seconds before firing. The light blinded the people on the bridge for a while. Then it became clear that the firing was alongside the boat but away from it. After this B-59 was ordered to return to the USSR. But what awaited her there? We leave that question for the next section.

articleEn: On the morning of 28 October 1962, Khrushchev's message was broadcast on Moscow Radio. He said that the weapons America called offensive would be dismantled, crated and returned to the Soviet Union. Kennedy called it an important and constructive contribution to peace. But part of the agreement was secret. America agreed to remove 15 Jupiter missiles from Turkey, and this was not made public at the time.

Kennedy had told his cabinet that if the same missiles could be traded away in a Turkey deal, the justification for invading Cuba would be weaker. The deal involved talks between Robert Kennedy and Dobrynin. Robert Kennedy had said informally that the Jupiters would be removed soon after the crisis. There is disagreement about Italy. Khrushchev wrote in his memoirs that it was included, and McNamara later ordered missiles removed from both places. The operation to remove the Jupiters was called Operation Pot Pie. It began on 1 April 1963 and was completed by 24 April. Meanwhile, on 20 November 1962, America announced the end of the blockade. The removal of Soviet Il-28 bombers had also been discussed.

Now back to B-59. On reaching the Soviet Union, several of the crew were reprimanded. One admiral told them it would have been better if they had gone down with their ship. Sources record this remark in that sense. Each captain submitted a report to Marshal Andrei Grechko, who was then acting as defence minister. Soviet authorities were angry that secrecy had been broken. But when it emerged that the submarines sent were diesel-electric, not nuclear-powered, the criticism eased somewhat. According to historian Alexander Mozgovoi, Grechko was furious on hearing this. He threw his glasses on the table and walked out of the room.

Arkhipov's wife Olga later said he spoke of these events very little. He felt his ordeal had not been appreciated. The whole story stayed hidden from the public for years. According to sources, these events became known to the public in 2002.
So the question is this: a decision made on a single night was meant to change the course of history, but can we accept this story as completely true?

articleEn: Was Arkhipov really the man who saved the world? In 2002 Thomas Blanton, director of the National Security Archive, called him exactly that: the man who saved the world. That same year Commander Vadim Orlov, who was aboard B-59, confirmed that the submarines carried nuclear torpedoes and credited Arkhipov with stopping the launch. But Orlov played down the situation. In his account Captain Savitsky did flare up in anger but then calmed down. So there are two versions of one event: one with a fierce argument over a launch and Arkhipov's refusal, the other with a captain who recovered after his anger.

Robert McNamara said in 2002 that we were very, very close to nuclear war, even closer than we knew at the time. Historian Arthur Schlesinger Jr. called it the most dangerous moment not just of the Cold War but of human history.

Now the other side. In 2024 historian Sergey Radchenko wrote that the evidence for the Arkhipov episode rests mostly on oral testimony, which was published by Svetlana Savranskaya. And when the Russian Ministry of Defense declassified documents in 2022, the Arkhipov episode was not mentioned in them. So what follows? We cannot say that nothing happened, nor that every detail is proven. The question remains open.

Arkhipov became a rear admiral in 1975 and was appointed head of the Kirov Naval Academy. In 1981 he became a vice admiral and later retired. He died of kidney cancer on 19 August 1998, aged 72. Some sources link the illness to his K-19 radiation exposure. In 2017 the Future of Life Institute gave him the first Future of Life Award, which his family received after his death.

After this crisis a Moscow–Washington hotline was set up so that leaders could speak directly in any future crisis. Later the Partial Nuclear Test Ban Treaty was also agreed, banning atmospheric nuclear testing. The lesson may be that big decisions sometimes rest in the hands of a few people, and that misunderstanding, exhaustion and silence together can raise the danger.
What do you think: was Arkhipov a hero, a myth, or both? Tell us in the comments.

shorts.titleEn: 3 Officers, 1 Nuclear Torpedo: The Vote Under the Sea
shorts.text: ایک فیصلہ، تین افسر، اور پوری دنیا کی قسمت! 27 October 1962 کو Cuba کے قریب Soviet submarine B-59 گہرے پانی میں تھی۔ اوپر US Navy کے 11 destroyers اور carrier USS Randolph اسے ڈھونڈ رہے تھے۔ انہوں نے signalling depth charges گرائے تاکہ submarine سطح پر آئے۔ اندر کسی کو معلوم نہیں تھا کہ جنگ شروع ہوئی ہے یا نہیں۔ Captain Savitsky کو لگا کہ شاید ہو چکی ہے، اور وہ nuclear T-5 torpedo چلانا چاہتے تھے۔ مگر launch کے لیے تین officers کی رضامندی ضروری تھی: captain، political officer اور executive officer۔ بحث چھڑ گئی، اور صرف Vasily Arkhipov مخالف تھے۔ کیا ایک آدمی کا انکار سب کچھ بدل سکتا تھا؟ پوری کہانی ہمارے channel پر دیکھیں۔
shorts.roman: Ek faisla, teen officer, aur poori duniya ki qismat! 27 October 1962 ko Cuba ke qareeb Soviet submarine B-59 gehre pani mein thi. Oopar US Navy ke 11 destroyers aur carrier USS Randolph ise dhoond rahe thay. Unhon ne signalling depth charges giraye taake submarine satah par aaye. Andar kisi ko maloom nahin tha ke jang shuru hui hai ya nahin. Captain Savitsky ko laga ke shayad ho chuki hai, aur woh nuclear T-5 torpedo chalana chahte thay. Magar launch ke liye teen officers ki razamandi zaroori thi: captain, political officer aur executive officer. Behas chhid gayi, aur sirf Vasily Arkhipov mukhalif thay. Kya ek aadmi ka inkar sab kuch badal sakta tha? Poori kahani hamare channel par dekhein.
shorts.descriptionEn:
On 27 October 1962, Soviet submarine B-59 was hunted near Cuba, and launching its nuclear torpedo needed three officers to agree.
Only Vasily Arkhipov opposed it.

shorts.titleEn: K-19: When the Reactor Cooling Failed at Sea
shorts.text: سمندر کے بیچ reactor کا cooling system اچانک فیل ہو جائے تو کیا ہوگا؟ July 1961 میں Vasily Arkhipov نئی Hotel-class submarine K-19 کے executive officer بنے۔ Greenland کے جنوب مشرق میں exercises کے دوران reactor کے coolant system میں بڑا leak ہو گیا۔ cooling system کام چھوڑ گیا۔ اسی وقت radio communications بھی ٹوٹ گئیں، اس لیے crew Moscow سے رابطہ نہیں کر سکتا تھا۔ کوئی backup system موجود نہیں تھا۔ Captain Nikolai Zateyev نے سات engineers کو حل نکالنے کا حکم دیا۔ انہوں نے ایک secondary coolant system بنا لیا، اور reactor کو meltdown سے بچا لیا۔ مگر Arkhipov کی زندگی کا سب سے بڑا امتحان ابھی باقی تھا۔ پوری کہانی ہمارے channel پر دیکھیں۔
shorts.roman: Samundar ke beech reactor ka cooling system achanak fail ho jaye to kya hoga? July 1961 mein Vasily Arkhipov nayi Hotel-class submarine K-19 ke executive officer bane. Greenland ke junoob mashriq mein exercises ke dauran reactor ke coolant system mein bara leak ho gaya. Cooling system kaam chhor gaya. Isi waqt radio communications bhi toot gayeen, is liye crew Moscow se rabta nahin kar sakta tha. Koi backup system maujood nahin tha. Captain Nikolai Zateyev ne saat engineers ko hal nikalne ka hukm diya. Unhon ne ek secondary coolant system bana liya, aur reactor ko meltdown se bacha liya. Magar Arkhipov ki zindagi ka sab se bara imtihan abhi baqi tha. Poori kahani hamare channel par dekhein.
shorts.descriptionEn:
In 1961, submarine K-19 lost its reactor cooling and radio contact near Greenland.
Seven engineers improvised a secondary coolant system and prevented a meltdown.

shorts.titleEn: Did One Man Really Save the World? Hero or Myth
shorts.text: کیا Arkhipov واقعی وہ آدمی تھے جس نے دنیا بچائی؟ 2002 میں National Security Archive کے director Thomas Blanton نے انہیں یہی کہا: the man who saved the world۔ اسی سال B-59 پر موجود Commander Vadim Orlov نے تصدیق کی کہ submarines میں nuclear torpedoes تھے، اور launch رکنے کا credit Arkhipov کو دیا۔ مگر Orlov نے منظر کم ڈرامائی بتایا۔ ان کے مطابق Captain Savitsky کا غصہ بھڑکا، لیکن پھر وہ پرسکون ہو گئے۔ 2024 میں historian Sergey Radchenko نے کہا کہ Arkhipov کے کردار کے ثبوت زیادہ تر oral testimony پر ہیں۔ تو سچ کیا ہے؟ ایک ہی واقعے کے دو انداز ہیں۔ پوری کہانی ہمارے channel پر دیکھیں۔
shorts.roman: Kya Arkhipov waqai woh aadmi thay jis ne duniya bachayi? 2002 mein National Security Archive ke director Thomas Blanton ne unhein yahi kaha: the man who saved the world. Isi saal B-59 par maujood Commander Vadim Orlov ne tasdeeq ki ke submarines mein nuclear torpedoes thay, aur launch rukne ka credit Arkhipov ko diya. Magar Orlov ne manzar kam dramai bataya. Un ke mutabiq Captain Savitsky ka ghussa bhadka, lekin phir woh pursukoon ho gaye. 2024 mein historian Sergey Radchenko ne kaha ke Arkhipov ke kirdar ke saboot zyada tar oral testimony par hain. To sach kya hai? Ek hi waqiye ke do andaz hain. Poori kahani hamare channel par dekhein.
shorts.descriptionEn:
Thomas Blanton called Vasily Arkhipov the man who saved the world, but accounts differ on how dramatic the B-59 moment really was.
A historian in 2024 noted the evidence relies mostly on oral testimony.
